deepDive.title: Atmosphere layers and the lapse rate — why mountains are colder
deepDive.body: In Class 7 you learned that mountains are colder because they're higher. Class 9 quantifies this. The atmosphere has FOUR layers — troposphere (0-12 km, where weather happens), stratosphere (12-50 km, where ozone lives), mesosphere, thermosphere. In the troposphere, temperature drops at a steady rate called the LAPSE RATE: about 6.5°C per kilometre of altitude. So at Manali (2050 m), it's roughly 6.5 × 2 = 13°C cooler than Delhi at sea level. At Mount Everest base camp (5400 m), 35°C cooler than coastal Mumbai. Why does this happen? As air rises, atmospheric pressure decreases, and rising air expands. Expansion costs energy — that energy comes from the air's own heat, so it cools. Same physics that makes a deodorant can feel cold when you press it (gas expanding rapidly).
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this after you're comfortable with how climate varies by location.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Class 11 explores why this lapse rate breaks down at high altitudes in the stratosphere — ozone heats the air, reversing the pattern.

deepDive.title: El Niño and La Niña — why India's monsoon failed in 2009 and again in 2015
deepDive.body: In Class 7 you learned that monsoons bring India's rain. Class 11 reveals that monsoons can FAIL — and the cause sits 12,000 km away in the Pacific Ocean. EL NIÑO: every 3-7 years, surface waters in the eastern Pacific (off Peru) warm dramatically (~2°C above normal). This shifts global wind patterns — including the jet stream that drives the Indian monsoon. Result: weaker monsoon over India, often a drought year. 2009 and 2015 were strong El Niño years; both saw deficient Indian rainfall and food price spikes. LA NIÑA is the opposite — cooler-than-normal Pacific waters, often stronger monsoon. Indian meteorologists at IMD Pune now forecast monsoons partly based on Pacific sea surface temperatures measured by satellite. Climate is a single global system — what happens in Lima can determine what happens in Lucknow.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this after you're comfortable with monsoon basics.
deepDive.nextStepHint: NEET / climate science: El Niño is part of the ENSO (El Niño Southern Oscillation) — Earth's biggest year-to-year climate driver.

deepDive.title: Biomes — how Earth is divided into climate zones
deepDive.body: In Class 7 you saw climates differ (polar, tropical, etc.). NEET expects you to know the SIX major terrestrial biomes — large ecosystems defined by climate. (1) Tropical rainforest (Western Ghats, Amazon) — hot, wet, biodiverse. (2) Temperate deciduous forest (parts of Himachal) — moderate temperature, seasonal trees. (3) Grassland (savannas of Africa, Indian terai). (4) Desert (Thar, Sahara) — low rainfall, extreme temperature swings. (5) Tundra (Ladakh winter, Arctic) — frozen, treeless. (6) Taiga (boreal Russia, Canada) — coniferous forests. Each biome has signature animal and plant adaptations. The same RAINFALL + TEMPERATURE conditions create the same biome across continents — convergent evolution. Indian Western Ghats and South American Amazon look similar despite ZERO direct connection.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this after you're comfortable with the polar/tropical adaptation examples in Class 7.
deepDive.nextStepHint: Marine biomes (coral reefs, deep sea, open ocean) parallel terrestrial ones — Class 12 ecology expands on this.
